title: The Golden Bowl
description: Published in 1904 and the last and most difficult of James's novels: the marriage of an American heiress to an Italian prince, and the affair that threatens it.
plot_or_argument: Maggie Verver, the daughter of a rich American collector, marries Prince Amerigo, whose former mistress Charlotte Stant then marries Maggie's father; the two resume their affair, and Maggie, by a campaign of silence and generosity, recovers her husband and manipulates the couple back to Europe.
historical_context: The 1900s: the American collector in London, the international marriage, and the great house and its treasures.
literary_significance: The Golden Bowl is the most formally daring of James's novels and the culmination of his late style: its treatment of marriage, adultery and the exercise of power through generosity is one of the great achievements of the modern novel, and it has become central to the criticism of James's ethics.

title: What Maisie Knew
description: Published in 1897 and the most daring of James's experiments in point of view: the story of a child's view of her parents' divorce and remarriage, told entirely through what she can understand.
plot_or_argument: Maisie is the pawn in the divorce of her parents, who each remarry and use her as a cover for their affairs; she is cared for by her step-parents, Sir Claude and Miss Overmore, and the novel ends with her choice to leave them and go home with her governess Mrs Wix.
historical_context: The 1890s: the English divorce law, the American expatriate world, and the Victorian and Edwardian literature of childhood.
literary_significance: What Maisie Knew is the central novel of the child's consciousness in English and a founding text of the modern novel of point of view: its method of showing only what a child can see made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of the limited perspective.

title: Daisy Miller
description: Published in the Cornhill Magazine in 1878 and the most famous of James's shorter works: the story of a young American girl in Rome whose innocence is read as impropriety.
plot_or_argument: Winterbourne meets Daisy Miller in Switzerland and again in Rome, where her unchaperoned walks with the Italian Giovanelli scandalise American society; he fails to defend her, she dies of Roman fever, and he realises too late what her 'innocence' meant.
historical_context: The 1870s: the American colony in Rome, the Grand Tour, and the American debate on the manners of the New Woman.
literary_significance: Daisy Miller is the founding American novella of the international theme and made James famous on both sides of the Atlantic: its analysis of the collision between American innocence and European convention created a permanent American literary type.

title: The Country of the Pointed Firs
description: Published in 1896 and the masterpiece of American regionalism: a summer in the Maine coastal village of Dunnet Landing, and the lives of the women who live there.
plot_or_argument: A visiting woman writer lodges with the herbalist Mrs Todd, visits the retired sea captain Littlepage, attends the funeral of the old sailor, goes with Mrs Todd to the reunion on Green Island, and hears the stories of Mrs Fosdick, Mrs Begg and the eccentric Elijah Tilley; the book ends with the departure of the visitor and the closing of the summer.
principal_characters: Mrs Almira Todd; the narrator; Captain Littlepage; Mrs Blackett; William Blackett; Mrs Fosdick; Elijah Tilley; Mrs Begg; Joanna Todd
historical_context: The 1890s: the decayed Maine port towns, the disappearance of the shipping trade, and the world of the unmarried and widowed women who remained.
literary_significance: The Country of the Pointed Firs is the finest work of American regionalism and one of the most perfect books in American literature: its structure, its treatment of women's community and its rendering of the speech of the Maine coast made it the model for the American regional novel and a central text of feminist criticism.

title: A White Heron and Other Stories
description: Published in 1886 and the best collection of Jewett's stories: the famous title story of a girl who refuses to betray a heron, and other tales of Maine country life.
plot_or_argument: Sylvia, a country girl, is offered ten dollars by a young ornithologist to show him the nest of a white heron; she climbs the great pine at dawn, sees the bird, and chooses silence and the bird's life over the money and the boy's approval.
historical_context: The 1880s: rural Maine, the new American interest in ornithology, and the literature of the country child.
literary_significance: 'A White Heron' is one of the most anthologised American stories and the founding text of American environmental fiction: its treatment of a child's moral choice between money and the natural world made it a permanent part of the American literature of nature.

title: A Country Doctor
description: Published in 1884 and Jewett's most directly feminist novel: the story of a young woman who chooses medicine over marriage, and of the cost of that choice.
plot_or_argument: Nan Prince, an orphan, is brought up by the country doctor John Leslie and chooses to become a physician; she studies in Boston, refuses the man she loves, and returns to practise in the Maine countryside, where the novel ends with her settled in her profession.
historical_context: The 1870s-80s: the first generation of American women physicians, the founding of women's medical colleges, and the New England countryside.
literary_significance: A Country Doctor is one of the first American novels about a woman's professional vocation and a key text in the history of American women's education: its picture of the medical training and the social resistance Nan faces makes it a founding work of American feminist fiction.

title: Deephaven
description: Published in 1877 and Jewett's first book: the summer two Boston girls spend in a decaying Maine seaport, and the old people whose stories they collect.
plot_or_argument: Kate Lancaster and Helen Denis take a house at Deephaven for the summer and spend it visiting the Captain's widow, the eccentric Miss Chauncey, the old sailor widows and the lighthouse keeper, and listening to the stories of the town's past.
historical_context: The 1870s: the post-war decay of the Maine ports, the summer visitor, and the American interest in local antiquities.
literary_significance: Deephaven founded the American regional novel of the summer visitor and established the form that Jewett would perfect in The Country of the Pointed Firs; it is a key text in the literature of New England and of American women's friendship.

title: The Awakening
description: Published in 1899 and the founding American novel of female emancipation: the story of Edna Pontellier's awakening to desire and selfhood in New Orleans and on Grand Isle.
plot_or_argument: Edna Pontellier, the wife of a New Orleans businessman, learns to swim, falls in love with Robert Lebrun, takes a lover in Alcée Arobin, moves out of her husband's house, and at the end walks into the sea at Grand Isle.
principal_characters: Edna Pontellier; Léonce Pontellier; Robert Lebrun; Alcée Arobin; Adèle Ratignolle; Mademoiselle Reisz; Doctor Mandelet; Madame Lebrun; Victor Lebrun
historical_context: The 1890s: Creole New Orleans, the summer resort of Grand Isle, the marriage law and the position of the married woman, and the American reception of French fiction.
literary_significance: The Awakening is the central American novel of female selfhood and one of the founding texts of American feminist criticism: condemned in 1899 and rediscovered in the 1960s, it is now read as the great American novel of a woman's refusal to be defined by marriage and motherhood.

title: Bayou Folk
description: Published in 1894 and the collection that made Chopin's reputation: twenty-three stories of the Creoles, Acadians and freedpeople of Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana.
plot_or_argument: The stories include 'Désirée's Baby', the terrible tale of a mother and her child of mixed ancestry; 'A No-Account Creole'; 'In and Out of Old Natchitoches'; 'La Belle Zoraïde'; and the comic dialect tales of the Acadian farmers.
historical_context: The 1890s: the Louisiana plantation and bayou country, the Creole and Acadian communities, and the new American local-colour market.
literary_significance: Bayou Folk is the finest American local-colour collection of the 1890s and the founding text of the literature of Louisiana: its treatment of race in 'Désirée's Baby' is one of the most powerful short stories in American literature.

title: A Night in Acadie
description: Published in 1897 and the second collection of Chopin's Louisiana stories: twenty-one tales, more openly concerned with sex and marriage than the first.
plot_or_argument: The stories include 'Athénaïse', in which a young wife leaves her husband and discovers her own desire; 'A Night in Acadie'; 'Regret'; 'A Respectable Woman'; and 'The Kiss', in which a woman calculates the value of her engagements.
historical_context: The 1890s: rural Louisiana, the new American woman, and the magazine market for local colour.
literary_significance: A Night in Acadie is the finest single collection of American local-colour stories of the nineteenth century and the book in which Chopin's treatment of female desire becomes explicit; it is central to the recovery of American women's writing.

title: At Fault
description: Published in 1890 at her own expense and Chopin's first novel: a story of Louisiana plantation life, divorce and remarriage.
plot_or_argument: Thérèse Lafirme, a widow who runs a plantation, falls in love with David Hosmer, a divorced man; the novel examines the Catholic prohibition of divorce, the alcoholism of Hosmer's first wife, and Thérèse's struggle between her faith and her love.
historical_context: The 1880s: the Louisiana plantation, the American divorce law, and the temperance question.
literary_significance: At Fault is the first novel of Louisiana plantation life by a woman and an early American treatment of divorce; it is a key text in the development of Chopin's realism and in the history of the American novel of marriage.

title: 'The Story of an Hour'
description: Published in Vogue in 1894 and one of the most anthologised American stories: the hour in which a wife learns of her husband's death and discovers her freedom.
plot_or_argument: Louise Mallard is told that her husband has died in a railway accident; she weeps, goes alone to her room, and feels a monstrous joy as she repeats the word 'free', and then her husband walks in alive and she dies of a heart attack — of joy, the doctors say.
historical_context: The 1890s: the American marriage law, the Victorian cult of the widow, and the short story as a form for the single revelation.
literary_significance: 'The Story of an Hour' is the most concentrated American story of marriage and freedom ever written and a founding text of American feminist fiction: its irony and its compression have made it one of the most studied short stories in the language.

title: 'The Yellow Wallpaper'
description: Published in the New England Magazine in 1892 and the greatest American story of the 1890s: the diary of a woman confined by her doctor husband for a 'nervous condition', and of the wallpaper she comes to see as alive.
plot_or_argument: The narrator is taken to a colonial mansion for a rest cure and forbidden to write; she becomes obsessed with the yellow wallpaper in her room, sees a woman behind its pattern, and at the end tears it off to release her, crawling round the room while her husband faints.
historical_context: The 1890s: the rest cure of S. Weir Mitchell, the medical treatment of women's mental illness, and the American woman's movement.
literary_significance: 'The Yellow Wallpaper' is the central American text on the medical treatment of women and one of the most important stories ever written about mental illness: it is read as a feminist indictment of the rest cure, as a Gothic study of confinement, and as a permanent challenge to the medical profession.

title: Women and Economics
description: Published in 1898 and the most systematic American feminist book of the century: an economic analysis of women's dependency and a programme for their emancipation through work.
plot_or_argument: Gilman argues that women are the only class in history maintained entirely by another class; that this dependency distorts both sexes and the home; and that women must be given access to productive work and to economic independence, with the domestic functions socialised and professionalised.
historical_context: The 1898: the American suffrage campaign, the new women's colleges and professions, and the evolutionary sociology of Lester Ward.
literary_significance: Women and Economics is the founding American work of feminist economics and one of the most influential feminist books ever written: it was translated into seven languages, made Gilman an international figure, and its analysis of unpaid domestic labour anticipates the whole modern discussion.

title: Herland
description: Published in the Forerunner in 1915 and the first sustained American feminist utopia: the discovery of a country inhabited entirely by women and the consequences for three male explorers.
plot_or_argument: Three American men find Herland, a country without men where the women reproduce parthenogenetically, have built a harmonious civilisation of gardens and education, and have no war, poverty or crime; the narrator falls in love with a Herland woman and the novel ends with the departure of the explorers and the pregnancy of his wife.
historical_context: The 1910s: the American suffrage movement, the First World War, and the utopian tradition of Bellamy and Morris.
literary_significance: Herland is the founding American feminist utopia and the most influential work of its kind before the 1970s: its vision of a society organised by women has shaped feminist science fiction from Marge Piercy to Ursula Le Guin.

title: The Man-Made World; or, Our Androcentric Culture
description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's most ambitious work of cultural criticism: an analysis of how the whole of American culture — art, religion, education, law and language — has been shaped by male dominance.
plot_or_argument: Gilman examines the 'androcentric' bias in literature, art, dress, cookery, medicine, education and government, and argues that human culture has been distorted by the exclusion of half of humanity and that the correction of this bias is the great task of the modern age.
historical_context: The 1910: the suffrage campaign, the new sociology of gender, and the American Progressive era.
literary_significance: The Man-Made World is a founding text of feminist cultural criticism and one of the first systematic analyses of what would later be called the social construction of gender.

title: Moving the Mountain
description: Published in 1911 and Gilman's first utopia: the return of an American who has been lost for thirty years to a country transformed by feminism and social reform.
plot_or_argument: John Robertson, presumed dead, returns to America in 1940 to find a country without poverty, with professionalised housework and childcare, communal kitchens, a rational education and full equality for women, and he is gradually converted to the new order.
historical_context: The 1910s: the Progressive era and the American utopian tradition of Bellamy's Looking Backward.
literary_significance: Moving the Mountain is one of the founding American feminist utopias and the most detailed picture of Gilman's social programme; it is a key text in the history of American utopian fiction and of the Progressive movement.

title: Up from Slavery
description: Published in 1901 and one of the great American autobiographies: the account of a life from slavery in Virginia to the founding of Tuskegee Institute.
plot_or_argument: Washington describes his childhood in slavery, his work in the salt and coal mines, his years at Hampton Institute, and the building of Tuskegee from a borrowed room to a great institution, and ends with his advice to the black youth of America.
historical_context: The 1856-1901: slavery and emancipation, Reconstruction, and the rise of the 'Tuskegee machine' in black American politics.
literary_significance: Up from Slavery is the central African-American autobiography of the post-Reconstruction era and one of the classic American narratives of self-making: it made Washington the most powerful black man in America and defined the politics of uplift for a generation.

title: 'The Atlanta Exposition Address'
description: Delivered at Atlanta on 18 September 1895 and the most consequential African-American speech of the century: the address in which Washington accepted social segregation in exchange for economic opportunity.
plot_or_argument: Washington tells the white audience that 'in all things purely social we can be as separate as the fingers, yet one as the hand in all things essential to mutual progress', and calls on black Americans to cast down their buckets where they are and to make themselves indispensable through labour and education.
literary_form: Oration (Atlanta Cotton States and International Exposition)
historical_context: The 1895: the Plessy v. Ferguson decision of the following year, the collapse of Reconstruction, and the rise of Jim Crow.
literary_significance: The Atlanta address is the founding document of the accommodationist strategy in American race politics and one of the most debated speeches in American history: it made Washington the leader of black America, and it set the terms of the argument that Du Bois would answer in The Souls of Black Folk.

title: The Future of the American Negro
description: Published in 1899 and Washington's fullest statement of his social philosophy: a series of essays on the past, present and future of black Americans.
plot_or_argument: Washington argues that the negro has advanced more in thirty years than any other race in history, that industrial education and the ownership of property are the true foundations of citizenship, and that the South's prosperity depends on the progress of its black population.
historical_context: The 1899: the disenfranchisement of black voters, the lynching campaigns, and the founding of the National Negro Business League.
literary_significance: The Future of the American Negro is the central statement of Washington's programme and a key text in the history of American race relations: it shows the strengths and the costs of the strategy of accommodation at the moment of its greatest power.

title: The Story of My Life and Work
description: Published in 1900 and the first of Washington's autobiographies, later revised and expanded as Up from Slavery.
plot_or_argument: Washington tells the story of his birth in slavery, his education at Hampton, the founding of Tuskegee, and his public career, in a version written for a subscription audience and filled with the details of the institution's growth.
historical_context: The 1900: the fund-raising for Tuskegee, and the American autobiography market at the turn of the century.
literary_significance: The Story of My Life and Work is a significant document of black institutional history and the first version of the most important African-American autobiography of the era; it is a necessary comparison text for Up from Slavery.

title: Working with the Hands
description: Published in 1904 and Washington's fullest account of the Tuskegee method: a book on the dignity of manual labour and the teaching of trades.
plot_or_argument: Washington describes the teaching of agriculture, carpentry, brickmaking, dressmaking and housekeeping at Tuskegee, and argues that the education of the hand is the education of the whole person and the foundation of black economic independence.
historical_context: The 1900s: the industrial education movement, the Tuskegee curriculum, and the American debate on vocational training.
literary_significance: Working with the Hands is the classic American statement of industrial education and a key text in the history of American education and of black self-help.

title: The Conjure Woman
description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's first collection: seven stories told by the old freedman Uncle Julius, in which the conjure tales of slavery turn the plantation tradition against itself.
plot_or_argument: Uncle Julius tells the northern narrator and his wife about the conjure woman Aunt Peggy and her spells — 'The Goophered Grapevine', 'Po' Sandy', 'Mars Jeems's Nightmare', 'The Conjurer's Revenge', 'Sis' Becky's Pickaninny' — and each tale records the cruelty of slavery under cover of a comic anecdote.
historical_context: The 1890s: the North Carolina plantation country, the American plantation tradition of Harris and Page, and the market for dialect fiction.
literary_significance: The Conjure Woman is the founding work of African-American fiction and a permanent rebuke to the plantation tradition: its frame narrative turns the minstrel tale into a record of slavery's cruelty, and it is one of the most important books in the history of American race and literature.

title: The Marrow of Tradition
description: Published in 1901 and the central American novel of the Wilmington coup of 1898: a fictional account of the white supremacist massacre that destroyed black political power in North Carolina.
plot_or_argument: The novel interweaves the lives of two families — the white Carters and the black Millers, who are half-sisters — with the political campaign that culminates in the burning of the black newspaper office and the massacre of the black citizens of Wellington.
principal_characters: Dr Adam Miller; Janet Miller; Major Carteret; Olivia Carteret; Jerry; Josh Green; Captain McBane; General Belmont; Sandy Campbell; Ellis
historical_context: The 1898: the Wilmington coup and massacre, the white supremacy campaigns of the 1890s, and the collapse of black political rights in the South.
literary_significance: The Marrow of Tradition is the first American novel about the Wilmington massacre and the most important American novel of white supremacist terror: it is the founding text of the African-American political novel and a permanent historical record of a massacre that American history tried to forget.

title: The Wife of His Youth and Other Stories of the Color Line
description: Published in 1899 and Chesnutt's second collection: stories of the colour line in the post-Reconstruction North and South, including the famous title story.
plot_or_argument: In 'The Wife of His Youth', Mr Ryder, a light-skinned leader of a society of mixed-race people, is asked to acknowledge the old black wife he married in slavery; he does so, and the story ends with his public recognition of her. Other stories include 'Her Virginia Mammy', 'The Sheriffs' Children' and 'A Matter of Principle'.
historical_context: The 1890s: the black middle class of Cleveland and the North, the 'blue vein' societies of light-skinned African Americans, and the American debate on racial identity.
literary_significance: The Wife of His Youth is the finest American short-story collection on the colour line and one of the founding texts of the literature of passing: its treatment of racial loyalty and class among black Americans is unmatched in the period.
